usage: 이것 + 은. Sets 'this' as what the sentence is about; contracts to 이건 when spoken.
이것 + 이. Marks 'this' as the doer/identity; in speech almost always becomes 이게.
이것 + 을. Marks 'this' as what the verb acts on; spoken form is 이걸.
이것 + 좀 softens a request when you hand over or point at a nearby object.
examples: 이것은 names something near you; the 은 frames it as the topic.
이것을 is the object form — note the 을 marks what was bought.
Sir/Ma'am, this is the new product.
Polished service register; 이것이 (not 이거) suits a clerk speaking formally.
nuance: 이것 is the full, written-leaning form of 'this thing,' pointing to an object physically close to the speaker (이/그/저 = here/by-you/yonder). Its everyday spoken twin is 이거; the meaning is identical, but the dividing line is register — 이것 belongs to writing, announcements, and polite service speech, while 이거 dominates casual talk. It pairs with particles to make 이것은/이것이/이것을, and a native ear expects those to shrink to 이건/이게/이걸 the moment the situation turns conversational. The classic English-speaker trap is reaching for 이것 to mean 'this' before a noun — but as a determiner you need 이 (이 책 'this book'); 이것 already bakes in '것/thing,' so 이것 책 is wrong. Also never use 이것 for a person; a human is 이분/이 사람, never a 'thing.'

usage: 그것 + 은. Frames a thing by the listener, or one already mentioned, as the topic; spoken 그건.
그것 + 이. Marks it as subject; in speech becomes 그게.
그것 + 을. The object form; spoken 그걸.
그것 + 때문에. Refers back to a thing or fact just raised as the cause.
examples: 그것 points to a thing nearer the listener than to you.
Here 그것 refers back to something already mentioned, not a physical object.
Formal/written tone; 그것이 (not 그게) fits a serious or business register.
nuance: 그것 is 'that thing,' and Korean splits English 'that' by distance: 그것 covers what is near the listener OR what both speakers have already talked about, while 저것 is reserved for what is far from everyone. Its casual mouth-form is 그거 (그게/그걸/그건). The near-synonym to keep straight is 저것 — the test is location of the referent, not just 'farther than this.' A huge use of 그것 that English speakers miss is the abstract 'that': referring back to a previous idea or statement (그것은 사실이 아니에요 'that isn't true') rather than a visible object. As with 이것, do not stick it before a noun — 'that book' is 그 책, never 그것 책 — and never use it for a person, who takes 그분/그 사람.

usage: 저것 + 은. Frames a far-off thing as the topic; spoken 저건.
저것 + 이. The subject form; in speech becomes 저게.
저것 + 을. The object form; spoken 저걸.
저것 + 봐. Casual exclamation drawing eyes to something distant.
examples: That over there is a mountain.
Both of you look at something far away — only 저것 fits this distance.
Please show me that one over there.
저것을 is the object form; you point across a counter at a distant item.
That thing visible far away is Namsan Tower.
저것이 (subject) naming a landmark in the distance.
nuance: 저것 means 'that thing over there,' reserved for what is far from BOTH the speaker and the listener — the third slot in the 이것/그것/저것 set (here / by-you / yonder). Its casual spoken form is 저거 (저게/저걸/저건). The synonym you must contrast is 그것: the choice is purely spatial — if the listener is close to the object, it is 그것, but if it is off in the distance for everyone, it becomes 저것. English collapses both into 'that,' which is exactly why learners overuse 그것 and under-use 저것; train yourself to ask 'is it near the other person, or genuinely far away?' Also keep 저것 (a thing) apart from 저기 (a place): 저것은 뭐예요? asks 'what is that object?', while 저기 뭐 있어요? asks 'what's over there (in that spot)?'

usage: Everyday spoken contraction of 이것. The form you actually use when shopping or chatting.
이거 + 가 fused into 이게. You almost never say 이거가.
이거 + 를 fused into 이걸. Smoother than the full 이거를.
이거 + 주세요. The default way to order or buy a nearby item.
examples: Bare 이거 with no particle — totally natural in casual speech.
이거 stands in for 'this dish/thing' right in front of you.
This one's cheaper, so I'll go with this.
Shows 이게 (subject) and 이걸로 (이거 + 로, 'with/by this') in one breath.
nuance: 이거 is the casual, mouth-friendly version of 이것 — 'this thing' near the speaker — and it is overwhelmingly the form you HEAR and USE in real life: shopping, ordering food, pointing things out. Meaning is identical to 이것; the only difference is register, with 이거 being conversational and 이것 belonging to writing or formal speech. It contracts naturally with particles into 이게 (subject), 이걸 (object), 이건 (topic), and 이걸로 ('with this'). The number-one English-speaker error is grafting English particle habits onto it: 이거가 sounds clumsy because Koreans fuse it to 이게, and the same goes for 이거를 → 이걸. Like 이것, it cannot sit before a noun (that job belongs to 이: 이 가방), and it should never label a person.

usage: Spoken form of 그것: near the listener, or the thing you both already know about.
그거 + 가 fused into 그게. The natural subject form.
그거 + 말고. Waving off one option to point at another.
Set phrase for correcting what the other person just assumed.
examples: Plain 반말; 그거 points at something by the listener.
Oh, that? I saw it too.
그거 refers to a thing/topic you've both already mentioned.
What do you mean by that?
그게 (subject) points back to what was just said, not a physical object.

usage: Spoken form of 저것: far from both speaker and listener.
저거 + 봐. Calling attention to something distant.
저거 + 뭐지. Half to-yourself wondering about a far object.

저게 (subject) names a building in the distance.

usage: A place far from both speaker and listener (여기/거기/저기 = here/there/yonder).
저기 + 에 for a static location or a destination.
Politely flags down a stranger or server without knowing their name.
Soft conversational opener / hesitation filler before a delicate topic.
examples: 저기 names a spot far from both of you; pair with 있어요 to locate things.
Excuse me, could I get a menu?
저기요 is the standard polite way to call a server.

Um... could we talk for a moment?
Sentence-initial 저기 cushions a hesitant or awkward request.

The synonym to separate is 저거 — 저기 is a SPOT, 저거 is a THING, so 저기 뭐 있어요? ('what's over there?') versus 저거 뭐예요? ('what is that object?'). usage: Question word for things, the full form of spoken 뭐.
무엇 + 을. Spoken form contracts to 뭘 or drops to 뭐.
무엇 + 이. In speech becomes 뭐가.
무엇 + 보다. Set adverbial meaning 'above all, most of all.'
examples: 무엇입니까 is a formal/written register; speech would say 이름이 뭐예요?
A polished service phrase; 무엇을 (object) keeps it courteous.
무엇보다 is a fixed expression — note it's one set phrase, not free 'what + than.'
nuance: 무엇 means 'what' (asking about things) and is the full, dictionary form that lives in writing, exam questions, signage, and formal speech (무엇입니까?). Its everyday spoken reduction is 뭐, with 무엇을 → 뭘 and 무엇이 → 뭐가; the meaning never changes, only the register, so the dividing line between 무엇 and 뭐 is exactly formal-vs-casual. The near neighbor to contrast is 무슨, which is NOT interchangeable: 무엇/뭐 is a standalone pronoun ('what?'), whereas 무슨 always modifies a following noun and asks 'what kind of' (무슨 책? 'what book?'). English speakers, used to one word 'what,' wrongly say 무엇 책 — but you must choose 무슨 책. Memorize the frozen idiom 무엇보다 ('above all'), where 무엇 fuses with 보다 and does not mean a literal comparison.

usage: 어느 + 것 (spoken 어느 거). Picks one item out of a known set.
어느 + 나라. Extremely common in 'where are you from?' questions.
어느 + 쪽. Choosing between directions or two options.
to what extent / about how much
어느 + 정도. Set phrase asking degree or rough amount.
examples: 어느 needs a following noun (것 here) — it can't stand alone.
어느 나라 is the natural Korean framing of 'where from.'
How much Korean can you speak?
어느 정도 asks degree — a fixed, very useful collocation.
nuance: 어느 means 'which' and is a determiner: it ALWAYS sits in front of a noun and selects one option from a limited, often visible set (어느 것, 어느 나라, 어느 쪽). The synonym you must not blur is 무슨: 어느 chooses from a known, bounded group ('which of these?'), while 무슨 asks 'what kind of' from an open field (무슨 음악 좋아해요? 'what kind of music?'). So 어느 영화 leans toward 'which (of the movies we're choosing among)?' and 무슨 영화 toward 'what (kind of) movie?' The English-speaker pitfall is using 어느 like the pronoun 'which one' on its own — but it cannot stand alone; you must attach a noun, and for 'which one' specifically you say 어느 것/어느 거. Learn 어느 정도 as a unit; it idiomatically means 'to what extent / roughly how much.'

usage: Reflexive pronoun pointing back to the sentence's subject.
자기 (+의) 일. The 의 usually drops, so people say plain 자기 일.
자기 + 가, typically inside a subordinate clause referring back to the main subject.
Affectionate address between romantic partners (자기 + 야).
examples: You should do your own work yourself.
Both 자기 (one's own) and 자기가 (the doer) loop back to the subject.
자기 = 'his own,' bound to the third-person subject 그.

자기야 is intimate couple-speak — only for a partner, never coworkers.
nuance: 자기 (Sino-Korean 自己, literally 'self-self,' 自 'self' + 己 'oneself') has two everyday lives. As a reflexive pronoun it points back to the subject already named in the sentence, usually third person — 그는 자기 방에 있어요 'he is in his (own) room' — and pairs habitually with 자기 일, 자기 잘못, 자기 자신. Separately, 자기(야) is a tender way couples address each other, like English 'honey/babe.' The synonym to contrast is 자신, which also means 'oneself' but is more formal/emphatic and combines into 자기 자신 ('one's very own self') or 자신감 ('self-confidence'). The sharp English-speaker pitfall is translating reflexive 자기 as 'myself': it almost never means the speaker — it tracks the grammatical subject, so it usually lands as 'himself/herself/themselves.' And socially, never aim 자기야 at a stranger, friend, or colleague; it reads as romantic and will feel jarring.

남 + 이. 'Other people' acting as the subject.
남 + 한테. 'To someone outside your circle' (남에게 in writing).
남 + 얘기. Chatter concerning other people.
examples: Don't worry about other people's business.
남의 = 'someone else's'; a very common warning-style phrase.
남 as 'outsider' — emotionally loaded, said after a falling-out.
남한테 = 'to other people'; note 한테 for a person target.
nuance: 남 is a native Korean word for 'another person / others' — people OUTSIDE your own circle — and it carries a real emotional charge of 'an outsider, someone unrelated to me,' not just a neutral 'other.' It sits in a pointed contrast with 자기 (oneself) and especially 우리 (us): saying 이제 남이야 ('we're strangers now') means an intimate bond has been severed, which is far heavier than English 'we're not close anymore.' Habitual collocations include 남의 일 ('someone else's affair'), 남의 시선 ('other people's gaze/judgment'), and 남 얘기 ('gossip'). The first English-speaker pitfall is confusing 남 with 남자 ('a man') — they overlap on screen but are unrelated in meaning. The second is using 남 for your own family or close friends; by definition 남 draws the insider/outsider line, so applying it to your inner circle either is wrong or signals a painful estrangement.

Calling your own family or close friends 남 — it marks outsiders, so it either misfires or implies a serious rift.
Missing the weight of 이제 남이야 ('we're strangers now'); it signals a broken relationship, not mild distance.

usage: First-person plural; also stands in for 'my' with family and in-group nouns.
우리 + 가. Marks 'we' as the doer.
우리 + 집. Koreans say this even for their own household.
Humble equivalent of 우리, lowering the speaker's group toward a listener.
examples: 우리 here includes the listener — an invitation.
우리 엄마 is 'my mom' in English, even though it literally says 'our.'
Humble 저희 toward a customer/superior; use it instead of 우리 when deferring.
nuance: 우리 is 'we / us / our,' but it ranges far wider than English 'our' because Korean frames family and group as shared property: 우리 집 ('my home'), 우리 엄마 ('my mom'), 우리 학교, even 우리 나라 — places English would render with 'my.' The crucial register partner is 저희, the humble form: when speaking to a customer, an elder, or anyone you defer to, you lower your own side by switching 우리 → 저희 (저희 회사, 저희가 하겠습니다). The dividing line is politeness/deference, not number. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is over-translating: 우리 엄마 almost always means 'MY mom,' not literally 'our mom,' so rendering it as 'our' sounds odd. A subtle second point: you cannot humble-shift 우리 나라 to 저희 나라 when speaking to fellow citizens, since the nation isn't 'lowered' between insiders.

Over-applying humility as 저희 나라 to fellow Koreans; 우리 나라 is the natural form among insiders.

usage: Direction or side near the speaker (이쪽/그쪽/저쪽).
이쪽 + 으로. Shows direction of movement — the guiding phrase.
이쪽 + 에. Marks a static location near the speaker.
이쪽 + 은. Polite way to present a person: '이쪽은 김 부장님이세요.'
examples: 이쪽으로 (direction) is the standard phrase for guiding someone.
Giving directions; 이쪽 points along a path, not at an object.
This is my colleague, Ms. Park Jimin.
이쪽은 politely introduces a person — softer than pointing with 이 사람.
nuance: 이쪽 means 'this way / this side,' the direction or area near the speaker, and belongs to the directional set 이쪽 / 그쪽 / 저쪽 (this way / your way / yonder way), mirroring the 이/그/저 system. Its workhorse collocation is 이쪽으로 오세요 ('come this way') for guiding people, plus 이쪽에 앉으세요 for seating them. A refined, very Korean use English lacks: 이쪽 politely points to a PERSON when making introductions — 이쪽은 ~예요 ('this is ~') — which sounds more courteous than bluntly indicating someone with 이 사람. The synonym/confusion to separate is 이것: 쪽 is about WHICH DIRECTION or side, while 것 is a thing, so 이쪽이에요 ('it's this way') is not 이거예요 ('it's this one'). Also note 그쪽 can mean 'you/your side' as a slightly distancing way to address someone, so the set carries social nuance beyond literal direction.
